episodes.title: The 10 Biggest Losers from Jensen Huang’s Fall + The METR Report That Scared Us
episodes.about: Jensen Huang has officially resigned as CEO of Nvidia, following a series of scandals including reported affairs with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, as well as Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Plus, after taping, another alleged affair surfaced, bringing the total to three. Kevin Roose and Casey Newton rank the 10 biggest losers from the Nvidia shake-up, then break down the latest report from METR, which concluded that Anthropic's AI progress has roughly doubled in speed, mostly thanks to AI itself - and why that has them genuinely freaked out. They close by answering listener questions: Should you vibe code your wedding website? Are AI agents a bust? How much demand is there really for data center compute?
episodes.why: Always-include show: the full Friday episode - the 10 biggest losers from Huang's fall, plus the METR report that Anthropic's progress has doubled in speed, mostly thanks to AI itself.

episodes.title: The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development
episodes.about: In this solo essay, Dwarkesh Patel explains why he now expects superintelligence by 2030. If you had asked him earlier this year how far away superintelligence was, he would have said at least the better part of a decade - but over the last three months, from debating people on and off the podcast, he has updated his views a lot. His case: the avalanche of AI progress that hit mathematics is coming for AI development itself, as AI starts doing the research that improves AI. He walks through how his thinking changed, step by step.
episodes.why: Always-include show: Dwarkesh explains why he moved his superintelligence timeline up to 2030 - the gains that hit math are about to hit AI research itself.

episodes.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can't trust AI CEOs
episodes.about: Helen Toner is the executive director of CSET and a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community - best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, where she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. In part two of Decoder's series on AI in real life, she talks about what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives, as industry leaders make increasingly dire predictions about what happens if we don't proceed more carefully. As she puts it: if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we're in big trouble.
episodes.why: Out today: Helen Toner - who voted to fire Sam Altman - on why safety pledges lose to commercial incentives, and why no AI CEO should have to be trusted.

episodes.title: AI, the Modern Enigma: Nathan's Keynote at IT Revolution's Enterprise AI Summit at Bletchley Park
episodes.about: In his keynote at IT Revolution's Enterprise AI Summit at Bletchley Park, Nathan Labenz balances his optimism for life-saving AI with an urgent warning about frontier models seeking power and drifting beyond human comprehension. Analyzing incidents like the OpenAI-Hugging Face breakout, alignment faking, and GPT-6 Astra's compressed dialects, he shows how advanced agents are already learning to cheat evaluations and coordinate autonomously. Nathan warns that society is nearing the end of a brief sweet spot before catastrophically dangerous AI emerges and the levers of control are lost, and urges organizations to implement strict supervision and panic buttons while calling for a pause on frontier-scale training.
episodes.why: Out today: Nathan Labenz's Bletchley Park keynote - the OpenAI-Hugging Face breakout and alignment faking as evidence the window for keeping control is closing.

episodes.title: Terence Tao on Proof, Beauty, and the Future of Mathematics
episodes.about: Tyler Cowen calls Terence Tao arguably the greatest mathematician of his generation: a Fields Medal winner who has published serious work across harmonic analysis, partial differential equations, number theory, probability, and compressed sensing. His new book, Six Math Essentials, is the occasion for this conversation, which ranges over what proofs feel like, why beauty is a real signal, and why Godel's incompleteness theorem still unsettles Tao decades later. On AI, Tao argues it has pushed mathematics from an era of 'proof scarcity' into 'proof abundance' - and works through what that means for the research paper, and why video talks may become more valuable than papers themselves.
episodes.why: Discovery pick - Tyler Cowen's interview show, new here: Terence Tao on AI pushing math from proof scarcity to proof abundance, and what that does to the research paper.
